-100.note: Alexander's successor kingdoms were in decline: the Parthians had taken Mesopotamia from the Seleucids, and Rome would absorb Seleucid Syria in 64 BC and, after Actium, Ptolemaic Egypt.

alexandria.blurb: Ptolemaic capital, with its Lighthouse, Serapeum and Museion. Ptolemy X had his mother Cleopatra III murdered in 101 BC and ruled with his niece-wife Berenice III until the Alexandrians expelled him in 88 BC.

image.caption: Reconstruction drawing of the Pharos, the Lighthouse of Alexandria, by the German archaeologist Hermann Thiersch, 1909.

rome.blurb: In 100 BC Marius, victor over the Cimbri, held his sixth consulship. When his ally the tribune Saturninus seized the Capitoline, Marius besieged him under a senatorial emergency decree, and a mob killed Saturninus in the senate house.

image.file: File:RRC 326.1 Gaius Fundanius depicting Gaius Marius triumphator.png
image.caption: Silver denarius of the moneyer Gaius Fundanius, 101 BC, showing Marius as triumphator in a four-horse chariot.

xian.blurb: Emperor Wu's palace-building peaked around 100 BC; by the end of his reign, palaces filled two-thirds of the walled city. After Zhang Qian's missions west, Chang'an was the eastern terminus of the Silk Road.

image.file: File:Round eave tile with cloud design, attributed to Weiyang Palace, Xi'an, Shaanxi province, China, Western Han dynasty, 3rd-2nd century BC, ceramic - Tokyo National Museum - Tokyo, Japan - DSC08507.jpg
image.caption: Round ceramic eave tile with a cloud design attributed to Chang'an's Weiyang Palace, Western Han, 3rd-2nd century BC; Tokyo National Museum.

seleucia.blurb: Founded as the first Seleucid capital, it fell to the Parthian king Mithridates I in 141 BC and became Parthia's western capital. It stayed a Hellenistic city, and its mint struck Parthia's first tetradrachms.

image.file: File:Tetradrachm of Mithridates II of Parthia, minted at Seleucia between 120 and 109 BC.jpg
image.caption: Silver tetradrachm of the Parthian king Mithridates II, minted at Seleucia between 120 and 109 BC.

antioch.blurb: Seleucid royal capital on the Orontes, a four-quartered Tetrapolis. Its citizens took sides in the dynasty's feuds, and in 83 BC they turned on their feeble kings and invited Tigranes the Great to occupy the city.

image.caption: The Tyche (Fortune) of Antioch, the city's patron goddess; Roman marble copy of a 3rd-century BC Greek bronze by Eutychides, Vatican Museums.

1.note: Two great empires spanned Eurasia: Augustus's Rome, early in the two-century Pax Romana, and Han China, where the regent Wang Mang would seize the throne in AD 9.

rome.blurb: Augustus was turning Rome from brick to marble. His Forum, with its Temple of Mars Ultor, had been inaugurated in 2 BC, and his grandson and adopted heir Gaius was consul for AD 1.

image.file: File:Forum of Augustus, Temple of Mars Ultor 2013.jpg
image.caption: Remains of the Temple of Mars Ultor in the Forum of Augustus, Rome; photo 2013.

xian.blurb: The Han capital, where Wang Mang ruled as regent for the boy Emperor Ping. In AD 1 he was made Duke of Anhan, 'Duke who made Han secure', the first duke in Han history.

image.caption: Rammed-earth foundations of the front hall of the Weiyang Palace, the Han emperors' palace in Chang'an; photo 2013.

el-mirador.blurb: The great Preclassic Maya centre, crowned by triadic pyramids such as La Danta, with raised white causeways running to Nakbe and El Tintal. It would be abandoned by about AD 150.

image.file: File:Flickr - archer10 (Dennis) - Guatemala 1828 - La Danta at the Mayan site of El Mirador.jpg
image.caption: The La Danta pyramid at El Mirador, Guatemala; photo 2007.

luoyang.blurb: The old Zhou royal city, where the Han founder first ruled before choosing Chang'an, was now the seat of Henan Commandery. Wang Mang would put one of his six state market offices here in AD 10.

image.caption: A painted Western Han brick tomb, reassembled in the ancient tombs museum at Luoyang; photo 2007.

100.note: Rome and Han China were both near their height: Trajan would take the Roman Empire to its greatest extent in 117, while the restored Eastern Han ruled China from Luoyang.

rome.blurb: Trajan, who entered Rome as emperor in 99, opened his third consulship here on 1 January 100. He was rebuilding the Circus Maximus, replacing wooden seating with stone; the work was finished by 103.

image.file: File:Circus Maximus seen from Palatine hill.JPG
image.caption: The site of the Circus Maximus seen from the Palatine Hill, Rome; photo 2014.

luoyang.blurb: Eastern Han capital of Emperor He, who in 92 closed the city gates and overthrew the Dou clan, leaning on palace eunuchs. In the palace workshop the eunuch Cai Lun would improve papermaking in 105.

image.file: File:Eastern Han Luoyang Mural of Liubo players.jpg
image.caption: Two men playing the board game liubo, detail of a mural from an Eastern Han tomb (AD 25-220) at Zhucun, Luoyang.

alexandria.blurb: Capital of Roman Egypt, a province held by the emperor through his own prefect, and a key granary for Rome. Tension between Jews and Greeks had brought riots in AD 38 and 66.

image.file: File:Monete romane, alessandria, in bronzo, con faro e imbarcazione, II secolo dc. 01.jpg
image.caption: Roman bronze coins of Alexandria showing the Pharos lighthouse and a ship, 2nd century AD; Numismatic Museum of Athens.

antioch.blurb: Roman emperors treated it as an eastern Rome, adding a forum, colonnades and a hippodrome modelled on the Circus Maximus. It was a chief centre of early Christianity, where converts were first called Christians.

image.file: File:Mosaic of Isiac Ceremony, from Daphne near Antioch, 2nd century AD, Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya, Turkey (36063955161).jpg
image.caption: Mosaic of a ceremony for Isis from Daphne, Antioch's suburb, 2nd century AD; Hatay Archaeology Museum, Antakya.

carthage.blurb: Refounded by Julius Caesar as Colonia Iulia Concordia Carthago, it was the capital of grain-rich Roman Africa and the second city of the western empire. Its amphitheatre was built around this time.

image.file: File:Roman amphitheatre of Carthage - view from above.jpg
image.caption: The arena of the Roman amphitheatre of Carthage, Tunisia; photo 2010.

seleucia.blurb: Under Parthian rule it was still, Tacitus wrote, a fully Hellenistic city, and the earliest Parthian iwans were built here in the early 1st century AD. Trajan would burn it in 117.

image.file: File:Tetradrachm of Vonones I, Seleucia mint.jpg
image.caption: Silver tetradrachm of the Parthian king Vonones I (reigned AD 8-12), struck at the Seleucia mint.
